questions.question: What is the synchronized keyword in Java and what does it prevent?
questions.title: synchronized Keyword in Java
questions.direct_answer: A `synchronized` method or block acquires an object's monitor. Only one thread at a time can hold that same monitor, so code using the same lock can protect a critical section. Releasing the monitor happens-before a later acquisition of it, which also provides visibility. It does not protect code that uses a different lock or no lock.

interviewer_intent.testing: Core multithreading knowledge—synchronized is the most fundamental synchronization mechanism in Java.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing what object the lock is acquired on, or thinking synchronized only prevents simultaneous execution without understanding the memory visibility guarantee.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the intrinsic lock concept and the difference between synchronized method versus synchronized block, including which object holds the lock in each case.

sections.title: Understanding synchronized and Thread Safety
sections.content:
The **`synchronized`** keyword combines two guarantees around a Java monitor. First, only one thread can own the **same monitor** at a time, so a critical section guarded everywhere by that monitor has mutual exclusion. Second, releasing that monitor happens-before a later successful acquisition, so earlier writes become visible to the acquiring thread.

An instance synchronized method locks `this`; a static synchronized method locks the declaring `Class` object. A synchronized block locks the expression you provide. The crucial design rule is that every access participating in one invariant must use the same lock. `synchronized` does not make an entire object or unrelated methods automatically thread-safe.

Keep the protected invariant clear and the critical section no larger than needed for correctness. A smaller block may reduce contention, but it is not automatically faster if it splits one operation incorrectly.

sections.title: One Thread at a Time on the Monitor
sections.content:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Thread A
    participant L as Monitor lock
    participant B as Thread B
    A->>L: acquire lock
    Note over A: runs critical section
    B->>L: tries to acquire
    Note over B: BLOCKED, waits
    A->>L: release lock
    L-->>B: lock granted
    Note over B: now runs safely
```

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|synchronized|~Uses a monitor|same-monitor mutual exclusion|unlock-to-later-lock visibility|instance, static, or block form
blue|Lock identity|~Must match protected state|instance method locks this|static method locks Class object|block locks its expression
emerald|Protected operation|~Keep invariant together|compound changes inside one region|all competing paths follow rule|unrelated code remains separate
violet|Trade-off|~Contention can block work|keep scope clear|do not hold over avoidable I/O|measure alternatives

sections.title: Wrong: an unsynchronized withdraw can overspend
Right: synchronized makes withdraw atomic
When to Use synchronized
sections.content: Use `synchronized` when several actions on shared state must behave as one operation and all paths can follow the same monitor rule. A transfer across two balances, for example, needs a consistent locking design for both values, not merely `synchronized` on one random method. An atomic class fits some independent single-value updates; concurrent collections provide atomic methods for some collection operations; locks provide additional policies. None is universally faster—choose from the invariant and measure contention.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Synchronizing on the wrong object**: Freshers often synchronize on different objects thinking they're protecting the same data—if Thread A locks on `lockA` and Thread B locks on `lockB`, both enter the critical section simultaneously. The lock object must be shared.
- **Synchronizing local variables**: Writing `synchronized(localVar)` in a method where each thread gets its own `localVar` instance provides zero protection—you need a shared lock object.
- **Forgetting static synchronized locks the Class object**: A static synchronized method doesn't lock instance methods, so instance and static synchronized methods can run concurrently, potentially causing issues if they touch shared static fields.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Monitor**: `synchronized` acquires one object's intrinsic lock.
- **Mutual exclusion**: applies only to code competing for that same monitor.
- **Visibility**: unlock happens-before a later lock of the same monitor.
- **Instance/static**: lock `this` or the declaring `Class` object.
- **Boundary**: a different lock—or no lock—gets no protection from this synchronized region.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`synchronized` protects a critical section by acquiring an object's monitor. If Thread A owns that monitor, Thread B cannot enter another section guarded by the same monitor until A releases it. An instance synchronized method uses `this`; a static synchronized method uses the class object; a block lets me name another lock.

It also creates a Java Memory Model edge: writes before releasing a monitor are visible after another thread later acquires that same monitor. The phrase 'same monitor' is essential. Synchronizing a writer on `lockA` and a reader on `lockB` gives no shared ordering. I choose the lock around the state invariant, and I keep the block focused without splitting an operation that must remain atomic.

beats.text: `synchronized` makes sure only one thread runs a block of code at a time. It works by grabbing an **intrinsic lock**, also called a **monitor**, on one object. Every Java object carries one. Another thread that wants the same lock simply waits its turn.

Without it, two threads can interleave their steps on shared data. One reads, the other writes, and an update vanishes. `synchronized` serializes those steps. They can't overlap, so the data stays correct.

items: A synchronized instance method locks on `this`, the current object.
A synchronized static method locks on the `Class` object instead.
A synchronized block locks on any object you name. That gives you finer control.

beats.text: Picture a `BankAccount` with a synchronized `withdraw` method. Thread A runs it, so Thread B waits for the account. Here's the non-obvious part. `synchronized` gives you two guarantees, not one. It blocks other threads, and a successful acquisition observes writes that happened-before it through the prior release of that same monitor. Freshers miss that second guarantee.

items: Locking on `this` exposes your lock. Outside code can grab the same monitor and stall you.
A long synchronized method keeps every waiting thread stuck, which kills throughput.

speakable_v2.cap: So `synchronized` is the simplest tool here. You get mutual exclusion and memory visibility from one keyword.

questions.question: What is a race condition and how does synchronized prevent it?
questions.title: Race Condition and synchronized Prevention
questions.direct_answer: A race condition occurs when an unsafe interleaving of actions on shared state can make the result incorrect. `synchronized` prevents a particular race only when every competing path guards the complete critical operation with the same monitor. It provides mutual exclusion for that monitor and a happens-before relationship between unlock and a later lock.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can explain race conditions with a concrete example, not just abstract theory.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying two threads run at the same time without explaining why concurrent access to shared data produces incorrect results.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the read-modify-write sequence at the CPU instruction level using the classic counter increment example, showing how operations interleave.

sections.title: What Race Conditions Are and Why They Matter
sections.content:
A **race condition** exists when a result can become wrong because concurrent actions on shared state happen in an unsafe order. The classic example is two threads performing `count++` and losing one update.

A `synchronized` block can fix that race when every read or update that participates in the invariant uses the **same monitor**, and the complete read-modify-write stays inside the block. One thread owns that monitor at a time, so the protected operations cannot overlap. Releasing the monitor also happens-before a later acquisition, providing the needed visibility.

The keyword is not a blanket cure. Synchronizing on different objects gives no mutual exclusion, and protecting only the write while leaving a related read outside the protocol may still be wrong. Choose the lock from the state being protected, not merely from the method where the bug appeared.

sections.title: How an Interleaving Loses an Update
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[Thread A reads count] --> B[Adds one in register] B --> C[Writes count back] A2[Thread B reads
the same old value] --> C2[Writes the same number] C --> D{Both wrote
the same value?} C2 --> D D -- Yes --> E[One update is lost] ```

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Race Condition|~Timing-dependent bug|interleaved read-modify-write|count++ not atomic|lost updates
blue|synchronized Fix|~Serialize access|one thread in section|atomic and visible|consistent result
emerald|Shared State|~The root cause|mutable and shared|multiple writers|needs protection
violet|Alternatives|~Beyond synchronized|AtomicInteger|ConcurrentHashMap|immutability

sections.title: Wrong: count++ races across threads
Right: synchronized serializes the increment
Where Race Conditions Occur in Real Systems
sections.content: Race risks appear where threads share mutable state and at least one operation writes it. For example, two in-memory inventory updates can both read five and both store four, losing one decrement. That outcome is possible, not guaranteed on every run. Protect the complete invariant with one lock, an atomic API, confinement, immutability, or a concurrent structure whose operation matches the need. A thread-safe collection does not automatically make a separate check-then-act sequence atomic; use its atomic methods or an external protocol.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Assuming single Java statements are atomic**: Freshers think `count++` is a single indivisible operation, but it compiles to multiple conceptual steps that can interleave. Only assignments of references and primitives up to 32 bits are atomic without synchronization.
- **Not synchronizing reads**: Protecting writes with synchronized but leaving reads unsynchronized still causes race conditions—readers might see partially updated state or stale cached values.
- **Using separate lock objects**: If Thread A synchronizes on `lockA` and Thread B synchronizes on `lockB` while accessing the same shared variable, both can enter the critical section simultaneously because they're not contending for the same lock.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Race**: an unsafe interleaving can break correctness.
- **Same monitor**: all competing paths must use one lock.
- **Whole operation**: protect the complete read-modify-write or invariant.
- **Two guarantees**: mutual exclusion and unlock-to-later-lock visibility.
- **Not automatic**: different locks or unprotected reads remain unsafe.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A race condition means concurrent actions on shared state can interleave and produce a wrong result. For example, with a shared counter at 10, two threads can both read 10 and both write 11, so one increment is lost.

A `synchronized` region fixes that race only when every competing path uses the same monitor and the complete read-modify-write stays inside the critical section. Then one thread owns that monitor at a time. Releasing the monitor also happens-before a later acquisition, so the next owner sees the protected writes. Synchronizing one method is not enough if another method reaches the same state without the monitor, and two blocks synchronized on different lock objects do not protect each other. The locking rule belongs to the shared invariant, not merely to one line of code.

questions.question: What is the difference between a synchronized method and a synchronized block?
questions.title: Synchronized Method vs Synchronized Block
questions.direct_answer: An instance `synchronized` method locks `this`; a static synchronized method locks the declaring `Class` object. A synchronized block locks the chosen expression for only the enclosed code. A smaller block may reduce contention, but it is not automatically faster: every access that belongs to the invariant must still use the same lock, and blocking I/O should normally not occur while holding it.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of synchronization granularity and the ability to choose appropriate locking strategies.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing you can specify a different lock object in a synchronized block, or thinking synchronized methods and blocks are completely interchangeable.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that synchronized blocks reduce the critical section size, improving concurrency by allowing multiple threads to execute non-conflicting parts of the method simultaneously.

sections.title: Synchronized Methods vs Blocks: Choosing Granularity
sections.content:
An instance synchronized method acquires the receiver's monitor for the method body. A static synchronized method acquires the `Class` object's monitor. A synchronized block lets the code choose both the monitor and the exact critical section.

Use a method when the complete method is one short operation on state protected by that monitor. Use a block when setup or slow work can happen outside the critical section, or when independent state has clearly documented independent locks. The block must still contain the whole invariant; making it too small can reintroduce a race.

There is no portable microsecond saving or guarantee that a block is 'way faster.' Measure real contention. A private final lock can prevent outside code from accidentally competing for the receiver monitor, but `synchronized(this)` is valid when it is the documented locking policy.

sections.title: Method Lock vs Block Lock
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB M[Synchronized method] --> M1[Locks whole method on this] M1 --> M2[Other threads wait
for the entire body] B[Synchronized block] --> B1[Locks only chosen lines] B1 --> B2[Rest of the method
runs in parallel] ```

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Synchronized Method|~Locks whole method|this for instance|Class for static|coarse-grained
blue|Synchronized Block|~Locks a region|choose the monitor|smaller critical section|finer control
emerald|Why Block Wins|~Less contention|lock only shared part|private lock object|avoid locking this
violet|Trap|~Locking on this|external code can lock too|use private final Object|prevents interference

sections.title: Synchronized Method vs Block
sections.content:
| Aspect | Synchronized Method | Synchronized Block |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lock Object | Implicit: this or Class | Explicit: any object you specify |
| Scope | Entire method body | Only the code inside the block |
| Flexibility | Fixed—can't choose lock | Choose lock per data structure |
| Performance | Holds lock longer | Holds lock only for critical section |
| Readability | Cleaner for simple cases | More verbose but more control |

sections.title: Synchronized Method vs Synchronized Block
When to Use Each Approach
sections.content:
Use a **synchronized method** when the entire method body accesses shared state and needs protection—like a simple getter/setter or a short operation that's entirely critical. It's clean and readable for straightforward cases.

Use a **synchronized block** when you have a long method where only a small portion touches shared data. For example, if your method parses a request, does validation, then updates a shared cache, synchronize only the cache update line.

Use different lock objects in synchronized blocks when protecting independent data structures—like separate locks for a user map and an order map in a service class. This allows threads working on users and threads working on orders to run in parallel. In high-throughput systems, reducing unnecessary lock scope can improve concurrency when contention is measured. Synchronized blocks also let you implement advanced patterns like lock ordering to prevent deadlocks by always acquiring locks in a consistent sequence.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Synchronizing on a local variable**: Freshers write synchronized on a variable declared inside the method, so each thread gets its own lock instance and no coordination happens—the lock object must be shared across threads.
- **Mixing method and block locks on the same object**: If some methods use synchronized method (locking on this) and others use synchronized block on a different object, they don't coordinate, and you still have race conditions.
- **Locking on a collection you're iterating**: Synchronizing on a list object while iterating doesn't prevent concurrent modification if other code adds/removes elements without locking the same object—use explicit lock objects or concurrent collections.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Instance synchronized method**: locks `this`.
- **Static synchronized method**: locks the declaring `Class` object.
- **Synchronized block**: chooses a monitor and narrower lexical region.
- **Correctness first**: protect the complete invariant with the same lock.
- **Performance is measured**: a smaller block can reduce contention but has no fixed speedup.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A synchronized instance method locks the receiver, while a static synchronized method locks that class's `Class` object. A synchronized block lets code name another shared monitor and limit the protected region to the operation that must be atomic.

For example, `synchronized void deposit(...)` locks the whole instance method. If the method first performs independent validation and only the balance update needs mutual exclusion, `synchronized (balanceLock) { balance += amount; }` can keep the unrelated work outside the critical section. The block is correct only if every access participating in the balance invariant uses that same `balanceLock`. I choose the form by ownership and clarity, not by assuming a block is always faster, and I avoid holding either form of monitor while doing slow I/O.

questions.question: What is AtomicInteger and when would you use it instead of synchronized?
questions.title: AtomicInteger vs synchronized in Java
questions.direct_answer: `AtomicInteger` provides atomic operations such as `incrementAndGet()` and `compareAndSet()` with volatile-style visibility for its value. Its implementation commonly uses compare-and-set and may retry under contention. It is often a good fit for one independent counter, but it is not guaranteed faster than `synchronized` and cannot by itself protect an invariant across several values.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of modern concurrency utilities beyond the basic synchronized keyword—java.util.concurrent is essential for production Java.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing AtomicInteger exists, or thinking it's just a wrapper around synchronized when it actually uses fundamentally different lock-free algorithms.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the non-blocking nature of CAS (compare-and-swap) and why it scales better under high contention—failed CAS operations retry immediately without blocking the thread.

sections.title: AtomicInteger: Lock-Free Thread Safety
sections.content:
**`AtomicInteger`** is a mutable integer whose supplied operations can be performed atomically across threads. `incrementAndGet()` prevents the lost update that a plain `int` or `volatile int` can suffer with `++`. `compareAndSet(expected, update)` changes the value only when it still matches the expected value.

JDK implementations use low-level atomic operations and may retry when another thread wins the update. This avoids owning a monitor for these simple operations, but 'lock-free' does not mean one hardware step, no retries, or always faster. Heavy contention can make repeated retries expensive.

Use it when one value can be updated independently, such as a best-effort request count. Use a lock or another higher-level design when several fields must change together or an operation contains a larger invariant.

sections.title: Blocking Lock vs Lock-Free CAS
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB S[synchronized] --> S1[Thread blocks
if the lock is taken] A[AtomicInteger] --> A1[Compare and swap] A1 --> A2{Swap succeeded?} A2 -- No --> A1 A2 -- Yes --> A3[Done, never blocked] ```

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|synchronized|~Lock-based|blocks other threads|any critical section|heavier under contention
blue|AtomicInteger|~Lock-free CAS|compare-and-swap|single-variable ops|scales better
emerald|When Atomic|~One variable|counters, flags|incrementAndGet()|no blocking
violet|When synchronized|~Multi-step invariants|compound updates|several fields|atomic class not enough

sections.title: AtomicInteger vs synchronized Counter
sections.content:
| Aspect | AtomicInteger | synchronized int |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mechanism | Lock-free CAS (hardware) | Mutex lock (OS-level) |
| Blocking | Never blocks threads | Blocks waiting threads |
| Performance | Faster under contention | Slower due to context switching |
| Use case | Single variable updates | Multi-variable compound operations |
| Memory overhead | One object wrapper | Intrinsic lock on any object |

sections.title: synchronized — Correct but Blocks Every Thread
AtomicInteger — Lock-Free Compare-and-Swap
When to Use AtomicInteger vs synchronized
sections.content:
Use **AtomicInteger** when you need a thread-safe counter, flag, or single integer variable that multiple threads update independently. It's perfect for request counters in a web service, rate limiters, metrics, or retry counts. The atomic package also offers **AtomicLong**, **AtomicBoolean**, and **AtomicReference** for other primitive and reference types.

Use **synchronized** when you need to coordinate multiple variables in a single atomic operation—like updating both a counter and a timestamp together, or checking a condition and then modifying state. AtomicInteger can't protect multi-step logic. For example, a check-then-act pattern like if count less than limit then increment requires synchronized or explicit locking to be atomic. In high-throughput APIs where thousands of threads increment a shared counter, AtomicInteger will outperform synchronized significantly. But if your critical section involves complex logic, I/O, or multiple fields, use synchronized or **ReentrantLock** for clarity and correctness.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using AtomicInteger for compound operations**: Freshers call get then set thinking it's atomic, but get followed by set is two operations—another thread can change the value between them. Use **compareAndSet** or **updateAndGet** for atomic compound operations.
- **Not understanding CAS retry loops**: The incrementAndGet method internally uses a loop with compareAndSet—if contention is extremely high, it can spin many times, though it's still faster than blocking.
- **Mixing AtomicInteger with synchronized**: If some code uses atomic operations and other code uses synchronized on a different lock to access the same logical state, you still have race conditions—pick one concurrency strategy and stick to it.
- **Assuming all atomic class methods are lock-free**: Some methods like lazySet have weaker guarantees—read the javadoc to understand memory visibility semantics.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Atomic operations**: `incrementAndGet`, `getAndAdd`, and `compareAndSet` update one value safely.
- **Visibility**: reads and writes have the memory effects documented for atomic variables.
- **CAS may retry**: lock-free does not mean a single attempt.
- **Performance is workload-dependent**: it is not guaranteed faster than a monitor.
- **Boundary**: one atomic field does not protect a multi-field invariant.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`AtomicInteger` gives me atomic operations on one integer, so `incrementAndGet()` is safe where `counter++` is not. Its implementation normally uses compare-and-set: update only if the value still matches what was read, otherwise retry.

That can avoid monitor blocking for a small independent value, but I would not promise it is always faster than `synchronized`; under heavy contention, retries also cost time. More importantly, it protects only that atomic operation. If I must debit one account and credit another as one invariant, two separate atomic integers are not enough. I would use a lock, a transaction, or a design that represents the compound change atomically.

questions.question: What is deadlock in Java and how can it occur?
questions.title: Deadlock in Java
questions.direct_answer: Deadlock occurs when a set of threads cannot progress because each is waiting for an action—often a lock release—that another thread in the set cannot perform. A two-lock cycle is the classic example. The waiting state may be `BLOCKED`, `WAITING`, or parked depending on the synchronization primitive, and unrelated parts of the application may continue.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of deadlock as the main pitfall of synchronized programming and multi-threaded systems.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Describing deadlock vaguely as threads waiting for each other without showing the concrete lock acquisition order that causes it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the classic two-lock example with bank account transfers and explain the lock ordering prevention technique—always acquire locks in a consistent global order.

sections.title: Understanding Deadlock: The Circular Wait Problem
sections.content:
**Deadlock** is a catastrophic state where two or more threads are stuck forever, each waiting for a resource (usually a lock) held by another thread in the group. No thread can proceed, and the application hangs indefinitely. It's the multi-threading equivalent of two cars blocking each other at a narrow intersection, neither able to reverse.

Deadlock requires four conditions to occur simultaneously:

- **mutual exclusion** — locks can be held by only one thread
- **hold and wait** — a thread holding one lock requests another
- **no preemption** — you can't forcibly take a lock from a thread
- **circular wait** — Thread A waits for Thread B's lock while B waits for A's

In Java, the circular wait is the key. Imagine transferring money between bank accounts: Thread 1 locks Account A, then tries to lock Account B. Simultaneously, Thread 2 locks Account B, then tries to lock Account A. Thread 1 waits for B (held by Thread 2), Thread 2 waits for A (held by Thread 1). Neither releases what they hold. The JVM can't detect or break this automatically—your application freezes until you restart it. **Lock ordering** is the classic prevention strategy: always acquire locks in a consistent global order (e.g., by account ID). When a global order isn't practical, `ReentrantLock` and its `tryLock` timeout let a thread back off and retry instead of waiting forever.

sections.title: The Circular Wait That Forms a Deadlock
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart LR T1[Thread 1
holds Lock A] -->|waits for| LB[Lock B] T2[Thread 2
holds Lock B] -->|waits for| LA[Lock A] LB --> T2 LA --> T1 ```

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Deadlock|~Permanent block|each waits on the other|circular wait|no progress ever
blue|Cause|~Nested locks|lock A then B|other locks B then A|opposite order
emerald|Prevention|~Break the cycle|global lock ordering|tryLock with timeout|fewer locks
violet|Detection|~Find it|thread dump|deadlock section|jstack / monitoring

sections.title: Wrong: lock order depends on the arguments
Right: always lock the lower id first
Where Deadlocks Occur in Production
sections.content:
Deadlocks happen when your code acquires multiple locks in different orders across different execution paths. The classic scenario is resource ordering problems: transferring between accounts, moving items between inventories, or updating related database records where different threads lock resources in opposite sequences. In Spring applications with nested synchronized methods, if Service A calls Service B while holding a lock, and Service B calls back to Service A, you risk deadlock. Database transactions can deadlock at the JDBC level if two transactions update rows in different orders. Even seemingly safe code like synchronized collections can deadlock if you synchronize on multiple collections in a chain of operations. The key is identifying where you hold one lock while requesting another.

Use **lock ordering** (always acquire in ID order), **lock timeout** with tryLock from **ReentrantLock**, or redesign to eliminate the need for multiple locks by using immutable data structures or atomic compound operations.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Nested synchronized blocks on different objects**: Freshers write code that locks object A, then inside that block locks object B, without realizing another method locks B then A—this creates the circular wait condition.
- **Ignoring lock acquisition order**: Not establishing a consistent global order for acquiring locks across all code paths that touch the same resources.
- **Thinking deadlock only happens with explicit locks**: Deadlock can occur with any blocking resource—database row locks, file locks, even joining threads in circular dependency patterns.
- **No timeout mechanism**: Using plain synchronized instead of ReentrantLock with tryLock means threads wait forever—there's no way to detect or recover from deadlock automatically.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Circular dependency**: Deadlock requires a cycle—Thread A waits for B, B waits for C, C waits for A (or any closed loop of dependencies)
- **Two locks minimum**: You need at least two locks for deadlock; single-lock systems can't deadlock (though they can have other issues like starvation)
- **Lock ordering prevention**: Always acquire locks in a consistent order across all threads—sort by object ID, memory address, or any total ordering
- **tryLock with timeout**: ReentrantLock offers tryLock that returns false if the lock isn't available within a timeout, letting you back off and retry
- **Thread dumps**: When an app freezes, taking a thread dump (jstack or kill -3) shows threads in BLOCKED state waiting for monitors, revealing deadlock cycles

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Deadlock happens when two or more threads are stuck waiting for each other forever. Neither can move forward. The classic example is two threads each holding one lock and trying to get the other's lock. Thread A locks Account X and tries to lock Account Y. At the same time, Thread B locks Account Y and tries to lock Account X. Thread A can't proceed until it gets Y, but Thread B holds Y and won't release it until it gets X. Thread B can't proceed until it gets X, but Thread A holds X. They're stuck in a circle. Your application just freezes. The JVM doesn't detect or break deadlocks automatically—you have to prevent them in your code. The standard way to prevent deadlock is consistent lock ordering. Always acquire locks in the same order everywhere in your code. For bank accounts, you might sort by account ID and always lock the lower ID first, then the higher ID. That way, no matter which direction you're transferring money, you acquire locks in the same sequence. No circular wait, no deadlock. Another approach is using ReentrantLock with tryLock. You can specify a timeout—if you don't get the lock in say one second, tryLock returns false. Then you release any locks you're holding, wait a bit, and retry. That breaks the circular wait. Freshers often nest synchronized blocks without thinking about order. They lock object A then B in one method, and B then A in another method. That's a deadlock waiting to happen. Always be aware of what locks you hold and what order you acquire them in.

beats.text: Deadlock happens when two threads each hold a lock the other needs. Thread A holds the first lock and waits for the second. Thread B holds the second and waits for the first. Neither one lets go. They're stuck forever.

Deadlock grows out of nested locking. Each `synchronized` block looks fine on its own. The trouble starts when two threads grab the same two locks in opposite orders. That forms a cycle that can't resolve.

items: Mutual exclusion: only one thread can hold a lock.
Hold and wait: a thread keeps one lock while it asks for another.
No preemption: nobody can force a lock away from a thread.
Circular wait: A waits on B's lock while B waits on A's.

beats.text: Picture a bank transfer between two accounts. Thread 1 locks account A, then account B. Thread 2 locks account B, then account A. Here's the sharp edge. Under load, both run at once with opposite arguments. Instant deadlock. The fix is a fixed order: always lock the lower account id first.

items: Nesting locks in different orders across threads invites deadlock. Define one global order and follow it.
If a global order isn't possible, use `ReentrantLock` and its `tryLock` timeout, then back off and retry.

speakable_v2.cap: So always grab multiple locks in one consistent order. The cycle can't form when every thread agrees on the sequence.

questions.question: What is the visibility problem in multithreading and how does synchronization address it?
questions.title: Visibility Problem in Java Multithreading
questions.direct_answer: A visibility problem occurs when no happens-before relationship requires one thread to observe another's write. If both paths synchronize on the same monitor, an unlock happens-before a later lock, making earlier writes visible after that acquisition. This is a Java Memory Model guarantee, not a command to flush every hardware cache.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Java Memory Model basics—synchronized does more than just prevent simultaneous execution, it also ensures memory consistency.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking synchronized only prevents race conditions through atomicity, without realizing it also solves the visibility problem through memory barriers.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the Java Memory Model (JMM) and the happens-before relationship—synchronized creates ordering guarantees that ensure writes before releasing a lock are visible to reads after acquiring the same lock.

sections.title: The Visibility Problem and Memory Consistency
sections.content:
A **visibility problem** occurs when one thread writes shared state and another thread is not required by the Java Memory Model to observe that write. The reader may keep seeing an older value or see related writes in an unexpected order.

`Synchronized` solves this only when both threads use the **same monitor**. A monitor unlock happens-before every later lock of that monitor. Therefore writes done before Thread A releases it are visible after Thread B acquires it.

This guarantee is defined in terms of observable ordering and visibility. JVMs may implement it with barriers and hardware coherence, but Java does not promise a literal 'flush all caches to main memory' algorithm. Use the happens-before rule when reasoning about correctness. For a simple publication flag, `volatile` may be enough; for a compound invariant, use a lock or higher-level concurrent utility.

sections.title: Why a Stale Cache Hides a Write
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    W["Thread A changes protected state"] --> U["A unlocks monitor L"]
    U -->|"happens-before"| K["Thread B later locks L"]
    K --> R["B observes writes ordered before A's unlock"]
    X["Plain unsynchronized access"] -. "no ordering edge" .-> S["stale or reordered observation is allowed"]
```

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Visibility problem|~Missing ordering|writer changes state|reader has no happens-before edge|stale observation allowed
blue|Same monitor|~Required protocol|writer unlocks L|reader later locks L|release orders before acquire
emerald|volatile option|~Simple publication|write/read one volatile field|visibility plus ordering|no compound atomicity
violet|Correct model|~Java Memory Model|reason with happens-before|not physical cache flushing|protect the full invariant

sections.title: Wrong: a non-volatile flag can be cached forever
Right: synchronized publishes the writes
Ensuring Visibility in Practice
sections.content:
Use **synchronized** to guarantee visibility when protecting compound operations or multiple related variables. Every exit from a synchronized block publishes earlier writes according to the Java Memory Model, and a later acquisition observes writes ordered before the release. For single variable flags like stop signals or initialization checks, use **volatile** instead—it's lighter weight than synchronized because it doesn't involve locking. Volatile ensures every write is visible when the required happens-before relationship is established and matching volatile reads receive the JMM ordering guarantee.

Use **AtomicInteger** and related classes from java.util.concurrent.atomic for thread-safe single-variable updates—they have built-in volatile semantics plus atomic operations. Be aware that final fields have special JMM initialization guarantees when construction does not leak `this`; a clear safe-publication mechanism is still the best design. In Spring beans, immutable configuration objects (@ConfigurationProperties) leverage this. Never rely on plain reads and writes to shared non-volatile variables—the JVM is allowed to reorder or cache them in ways that violate your expectations of sequential execution.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Synchronizing writes but not reads**: Freshers protect the write with synchronized but leave reads unsynchronized—reads will still see stale cached values because they don't acquire the lock that triggers cache invalidation.
- **Assuming volatile solves race conditions**: Volatile guarantees visibility but not atomicity—count plus plus on a volatile int still has a race condition because it's three operations (read, increment, write).
- **Ignoring happens-before**: Not realizing that synchronized creates ordering guarantees between threads—writes before releasing a lock are visible to subsequent acquisitions of the same lock.
- **Over-relying on eventual consistency**: Thinking writes will eventually become visible without synchronization—the JMM provides no time bound, so threads might spin forever seeing stale values.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Visibility problem**: another thread is not required to observe a write without proper ordering.
- **Same monitor**: unlock happens-before a later lock of that monitor.
- **Both sides participate**: locking only the writer does not order a plain reader.
- **Specification model**: happens-before, not literal cache flush/invalidation.
- **Choose by operation**: volatile for suitable publication; locking for compound state.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A visibility problem means Thread A changes shared data but Thread B has no synchronization rule requiring it to observe that change. `synchronized` creates the rule when both sides use the same monitor: A's unlock happens-before B's later lock, so B sees the writes that came before the unlock.

I avoid explaining this as 'the JVM flushes every cache to main memory.' That is a hardware story, not the Java guarantee. The portable rule is happens-before. If the state is a simple stop or publication flag, `volatile` may express the hand-off. If several fields form one invariant, I protect the complete operation with the same lock.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app processing order requests with multiple threads
familiarity_anchors: reading a newspaper from yesterday vs today's edition
a whiteboard update not yet visible to everyone in the room
a shared Google Doc that hasn't synced yet
speakable_v2.hook: `synchronized` does more than block threads. It also makes sure threads see each other's latest writes, not stale cached copies.

beats.text: The visibility problem is when Thread A writes a value, but Thread B keeps seeing the old one. Each CPU core has its own cache. So the two threads look at the same variable, yet read different values.

The Java Memory Model does not require a reader to observe another thread's write without a happens-before relationship. Hardware caches and compiler or processor transformations must all obey the guarantees once that relationship exists.

items: On lock release, the thread publishes earlier writes according to the Java Memory Model.
On lock acquire, the next thread observes the writes ordered before the acquisition.
That pairing gives you the happens-before guarantee from the Java Memory Model.

beats.text: Picture a thread looping while a `running` flag stays true. Another thread sets that flag to false. Here's the non-obvious part. The looping thread can cache the old true value and spin forever. It never sees the change. Marking the flag `volatile`, or guarding it with `synchronized`, forces a fresh read.

items: Syncing the write but not the read still breaks. An unsynced read can see a stale value.
Without `volatile` or `synchronized`, one thread's flag change might never reach another.

speakable_v2.cap: So `synchronized` gives you both guarantees at once. You get mutual exclusion and memory visibility from one keyword.
